question: Which test do courts most commonly apply to decide whether an item installed by a property owner has become a fixture (real property) rather than remaining personal property?
choice_a: The MARIA test: method of attachment, adaptability to the property, relationship of the parties, intention, and agreement between the parties
choice_b: Whether the item was purchased before or after the property was listed for sale
choice_c: Whether the item cost more than $500
choice_d: Whether the item is mentioned in the property tax assessment
explanation: Courts typically weigh the method/permanence of attachment, adaptability of the item to the property's use, the relationship between the parties, the intention of the person who installed it, and any agreement addressing the item to determine whether it is a fixture that conveys with the real property.

question: A tenant installs specialized display shelving in a rented retail space to run her business. What is this shelving generally classified as?
choice_a: A fixture that automatically becomes the landlord's property the moment it is installed
choice_b: A trade fixture, which the tenant may remove before the lease ends as long as she repairs any resulting damage
choice_c: Real property that cannot be removed under any circumstances
choice_d: An encroachment on the landlord's property
explanation: Trade fixtures installed by a commercial tenant for business purposes remain the tenant's personal property and may be removed before the lease expires, subject to an obligation to repair any damage caused by removal.

question: A farm tenant plants and cultivates a corn crop during the lease term. What are annually cultivated crops like this legally called, and who generally has the right to harvest them?
choice_a: Riparian rights; they automatically transfer to the landlord
choice_b: Appurtenances; they pass with title to any new owner
choice_c: Emblements; the tenant generally retains the right to harvest them even after the lease ends
choice_d: Chattels real; they are destroyed upon lease termination
explanation: Cultivated annual crops are classified as emblements (fructus industriales) and are treated as personal property; a tenant farmer typically retains the right to enter and harvest them even if the lease has already ended.

question: Which document is used to convey ownership of personal property, as opposed to a deed used for real property?
choice_a: A deed of trust
choice_b: An easement agreement
choice_c: A recorded plat
choice_d: A bill of sale
explanation: A bill of sale is the instrument used to transfer title to personal property (chattels); a deed is used to convey an interest in real property.

question: Real property is best defined as which of the following?
choice_a: Land, everything permanently attached to it, and the legal rights, interests, and appurtenances that go with ownership
choice_b: Only the physical soil and minerals beneath the surface
choice_c: Any item that can be moved from one location to another
choice_d: Only structures built on land, excluding the land itself
explanation: Real property includes land, permanent improvements and attachments (fixtures), and the bundle of legal rights (such as the right to possess, use, transfer, encumber, and exclude) that accompany ownership.

question: How can real property become personal property?
choice_a: By recording a new deed
choice_b: Through severance, such as cutting timber, extracting minerals, or detaching a fixture from the land
choice_c: By obtaining a certificate of occupancy
choice_d: By paying off a mortgage lien
explanation: Severance occurs when something that was part of the real property is detached from it, such as harvested timber, extracted minerals, or a fixture that is removed, converting it into personal property.

question: In a metes and bounds legal description, what is the significance of the 'point of beginning'?
choice_a: It is the geographic center of the parcel
choice_b: It marks the location of the principal meridian
choice_c: It is the fixed starting point from which the boundary description proceeds and to which it must ultimately return to close the description
choice_d: It identifies the block number within a recorded subdivision
explanation: A metes and bounds description starts at an identifiable point of beginning, traces the boundary using distances and directions (or natural/artificial monuments), and must return to that same point of beginning to properly close the description.

question: The lot and block (recorded plat) method of legal description primarily relies on which reference?
choice_a: Distances and bearings measured from a point of beginning
choice_b: Township, range, and section numbers from the government survey
choice_c: The elevation of the parcel above a fixed datum
choice_d: A subdivision plat map recorded in the public records, identifying the lot number, block number, and subdivision name
explanation: The lot and block system references a recorded plat map that shows individual numbered lots within numbered blocks of a named subdivision; the legal description simply cites the lot, block, subdivision name, and the recording information for that plat.

question: In the government (rectangular) survey system, what is a township?
choice_a: A square parcel measuring six miles by six miles, containing 36 square miles and divided into 36 numbered sections
choice_b: A single square mile of land equal to 640 acres
choice_c: A quarter-section of land equal to 160 acres
choice_d: The area between two adjoining principal meridians
explanation: A township in the rectangular survey system is a six-mile-by-six-mile square (36 square miles), created by the intersection of township lines (running east-west) and range lines (running north-south), and it is divided into 36 numbered sections.

question: In the government rectangular survey system, how many acres are contained in one full section?
choice_a: 160 acres
choice_b: 640 acres, since a section is one square mile
choice_c: 36 acres
choice_d: 43,560 acres
explanation: A section is one square mile, and one square mile equals 640 acres. There are 36 sections in each township.

question: A parcel is described as the 'NE 1/4 of the SW 1/4' of a section. How many acres does this parcel contain?
choice_a: 160 acres
choice_b: 10 acres
choice_c: 40 acres, because each quarter of a quarter-section is one-sixteenth of a 640-acre section
choice_d: 80 acres
explanation: A section contains 640 acres. A quarter-section is 160 acres, and a quarter of that quarter-section is 40 acres (640 ÷ 4 ÷ 4 = 40).

question: How many square feet are in one acre of land?
choice_a: 36,000 square feet
choice_b: 5,280 square feet
choice_c: 10,890 square feet
choice_d: 43,560 square feet
explanation: One acre is universally defined as 43,560 square feet, a standard unit of land measurement used across legal descriptions and appraisal calculations.

question: What is a benchmark, as the term is used in land surveying?
choice_a: A permanent reference marker of known location and elevation, established by government survey, used to measure elevations of nearby points
choice_b: The boundary line between two adjoining lots
choice_c: A private restriction limiting how a parcel may be used
choice_d: The center point of a section in the rectangular survey system
explanation: A benchmark is a permanent marker at a known location and elevation, set by a government survey, that surveyors use as a reference point for determining the elevation of other points, including in vertical (air lot) descriptions such as those used for condominiums.

question: Why does a valid legal description matter for a deed conveying real property?
choice_a: It determines the buyer's credit score at closing
choice_b: It uniquely and precisely identifies the exact parcel being conveyed, distinguishing it from all other land
choice_c: It sets the property's assessed tax value
choice_d: It is only required for commercial property, not residential property
explanation: A legal description must identify a parcel of land with enough precision and certainty that it cannot be confused with any other parcel; a street address alone is generally not considered sufficiently precise for a deed.

question: What distinguishes a general lien from a specific lien?
choice_a: A general lien is always voluntary, while a specific lien is always involuntary
choice_b: A general lien can never be foreclosed, while a specific lien can always be foreclosed
choice_c: A general lien attaches to all of a debtor's property, while a specific lien attaches only to one particular piece of property
choice_d: A general lien only applies to personal property, while a specific lien only applies to real property
explanation: A general lien, such as a judgment lien or IRS tax lien, attaches to all property owned by the debtor, whereas a specific lien, such as a mortgage or a mechanic's lien, attaches only to the particular property that is the subject of the debt.

question: A mortgage is an example of which type of lien?
choice_a: An involuntary, general lien
choice_b: A statutory lien that arises automatically without the owner's consent
choice_c: A lien that has no priority against other creditors
choice_d: A voluntary, specific lien, since the borrower agrees to it and it applies only to the mortgaged property
explanation: A mortgage lien is voluntary because the property owner agrees to grant it as security for a loan, and it is specific because it attaches only to the particular property pledged as collateral.

question: A contractor who is not paid for work performed on a property may file which type of lien to secure payment?
choice_a: A mechanic's lien
choice_b: A judgment lien
choice_c: An easement
choice_d: A license
explanation: A mechanic's lien is an involuntary, specific lien that contractors, subcontractors, or suppliers may file against a property when they are not paid for labor or materials furnished to improve it.

question: When multiple liens are recorded against the same property, which lien is generally given the highest priority for repayment regardless of its recording date?
choice_a: The first mortgage recorded
choice_b: A real property tax lien
choice_c: A judgment lien
choice_d: A mechanic's lien
explanation: Real property tax liens generally take priority over all other liens regardless of when they were recorded, because governments require tax revenue to be secured ahead of private debts; most other liens follow a 'first in time, first in right' recording priority.

question: What is the key difference between an easement appurtenant and an easement in gross?
choice_a: An easement appurtenant always requires payment, while an easement in gross is always free
choice_b: An easement appurtenant is temporary, while an easement in gross is permanent
choice_c: An easement appurtenant benefits an adjoining parcel of land and runs with the land, while an easement in gross benefits a specific person or entity rather than a parcel of land
choice_d: An easement appurtenant applies only to commercial property
explanation: An easement appurtenant attaches to and benefits a dominant estate (an adjoining parcel) and automatically transfers with the land when it is sold, while an easement in gross benefits a particular person or company, such as a utility company, rather than a neighboring parcel.

question: In an easement appurtenant, what are the dominant and servient estates?
choice_a: The dominant estate bears the burden, while the servient estate receives the benefit
choice_b: Both estates equally share the burden and benefit
choice_c: Only the servient estate has legal title to the easement
choice_d: The dominant estate benefits from the easement, while the servient estate bears the burden of allowing the use
explanation: In an easement appurtenant, the parcel that receives the benefit of the easement is called the dominant estate (or dominant tenement), and the parcel burdened by allowing the use is called the servient estate (or servient tenement).

question: An easement can be created through long-term, open, continuous, and hostile use of another's land without permission, for a period set by law. What is this type of easement called?
choice_a: An easement by prescription
choice_b: An easement by necessity
choice_c: An easement in gross
choice_d: A license
explanation: An easement by prescription arises when someone uses another's land openly, notoriously, continuously, and without the owner's permission (hostile to the owner's interest) for the period of time required by law, similar in concept to adverse possession but granting only a right of use rather than title.

question: How does a license to use land differ from an easement?
choice_a: A license is permanent and cannot be revoked, while an easement can be revoked at any time
choice_b: A license is a personal, revocable permission to use land that does not create an interest in the property or run with the land, while an easement is a nonpossessory interest in land
choice_c: A license automatically transfers with the sale of the land, while an easement does not
choice_d: A license requires a recorded deed, while an easement never needs to be recorded
explanation: A license is merely personal permission granted by a landowner to use the property for a specific purpose; it is generally revocable at the will of the owner and does not create a property interest or transfer with the land, unlike an easement.

question: A neighbor's fence is built two feet over the property line onto an adjoining owner's lot. What is this situation called?
choice_a: An emblement
choice_b: A riparian right
choice_c: An encroachment
choice_d: A deed restriction
explanation: An encroachment occurs when a structure or improvement, such as a fence, wall, or building overhang, extends onto an adjoining owner's property without permission, which can cloud title and lead to disputes.

question: Which of the following is generally required to establish title to land through adverse possession?
choice_a: A single visit to the property once a year
choice_b: Written permission from the record owner
choice_c: Payment of one year's property taxes only
choice_d: Possession that is open and notorious, continuous, hostile to the true owner's interest, and actual, maintained for a statutory period of time
explanation: Adverse possession generally requires possession that is open and notorious, continuous and uninterrupted, hostile (without the owner's permission), and actual, exclusive occupation, all maintained for a period of time set by law; some jurisdictions add requirements such as color of title or payment of property taxes.

question: How can a pending probate proceeding affect a property's title?
choice_a: It can create a temporary encumbrance or cloud on title because ownership cannot be fully transferred until the estate is administered and the court authorizes conveyance
choice_b: It automatically extinguishes any existing mortgage on the property
choice_c: It has no effect on title because probate applies only to personal belongings, never real property
choice_d: It immediately transfers full marketable title to the heirs without any court involvement
explanation: When a property owner dies, the property typically must pass through probate, during which the court oversees administration of the estate; until that process concludes and proper authority to convey is established, the pending probate can act as a potential encumbrance on marketable title.

question: A landlord grants a tenant a leasehold estate under a signed lease. From the standpoint of the landlord's fee title, what is this leasehold?
choice_a: A form of easement in gross
choice_b: A potential encumbrance, since it gives the tenant an exclusive right of possession that limits the owner's own use of the property during the lease term
choice_c: A type of mechanic's lien
choice_d: A government survey monument
explanation: A lease creates a leasehold estate in the tenant, giving the tenant a temporary but exclusive right to possess and use the property; because it restricts the landlord's own possessory rights during the lease term, an existing lease is considered a potential encumbrance on the fee owner's title.

question: Mineral rights, such as the right to extract oil, gas, or coal beneath a parcel, can be handled in which way?
choice_a: They must always remain permanently attached to surface ownership and can never be sold separately
choice_b: They automatically transfer to the government the moment a deed is recorded
choice_c: They can be severed from the surface rights and sold or leased separately from the rest of the property
choice_d: They are extinguished whenever the surface is sold
explanation: Subsurface mineral rights are a distinct property interest that can be severed (separated) from surface rights, allowing an owner to sell or lease the mineral estate while retaining or transferring the surface estate separately.

question: What are air rights, in the context of real property ownership?
choice_a: The right to draw water from an adjacent river
choice_b: The right to extract minerals from beneath the surface
choice_c: A type of easement that always benefits the general public
choice_d: The right to use, control, or develop the space above a parcel of land, which can be sold or leased separately from the land itself
explanation: Air rights refer to the right to use and control the space above a parcel of land; like mineral rights, air rights can be severed from the surface estate and sold, leased, or developed separately, as is often done above rail lines or in dense urban areas.

question: An owner of land bordering a navigable river has rights to reasonable use of the water and access to it. What are these rights called?
choice_a: Riparian rights
choice_b: Littoral rights
choice_c: Prescriptive rights
choice_d: Emblements
explanation: Riparian rights belong to owners of land bordering a flowing waterway, such as a river or stream, and generally include the right to reasonable use of the water and access to it, subject to the rights of other riparian owners.

question: How do littoral rights differ from riparian rights?
choice_a: Littoral rights apply only to underground water, while riparian rights apply only to rainwater
choice_b: Littoral rights belong to owners of land bordering large, non-flowing bodies of water such as oceans and lakes, while riparian rights belong to owners bordering flowing waterways such as rivers and streams
choice_c: Littoral rights are always superior to riparian rights
choice_d: There is no meaningful difference between the two terms
explanation: Littoral rights apply to property bordering large, substantially non-flowing bodies of water, such as oceans, seas, and lakes, while riparian rights apply to property bordering flowing waters such as rivers and streams.

question: Ownership of real property by a single individual or entity, with no co-owners, is known as which form of ownership?
choice_a: Tenancy in common
choice_b: Joint tenancy
choice_c: Ownership in severalty
choice_d: Tenancy by the entirety
explanation: Ownership in severalty means the property is owned by one person or single legal entity alone, 'severed' from ownership by anyone else, and it carries no co-ownership rights such as survivorship.

question: Which statement correctly describes tenancy in common?
choice_a: All co-owners must hold exactly equal shares and the last surviving owner automatically receives the entire property
choice_b: It can only be created between married spouses
choice_c: Each owner holds a physically separate, fenced-off portion of the property
choice_d: Two or more owners hold undivided interests in the property, which may be unequal in size, and there is no right of survivorship between them
explanation: In a tenancy in common, two or more owners each hold an undivided fractional interest in the whole property, the shares can be unequal, and when one tenant in common dies, that owner's interest passes to their heirs or as directed by will rather than automatically to the surviving co-owners.

question: What defining feature distinguishes a joint tenancy from a tenancy in common?
choice_a: Joint tenancy includes the right of survivorship, meaning a deceased joint tenant's interest passes automatically to the surviving joint tenant(s) rather than to heirs
choice_b: Joint tenancy allows owners to hold unequal shares, while tenancy in common requires equal shares
choice_c: Joint tenancy can only be formed by a court order
choice_d: Joint tenancy automatically terminates after five years
explanation: The right of survivorship is the hallmark of joint tenancy: when a joint tenant dies, their interest passes automatically and immediately to the surviving joint tenant(s), bypassing probate and the deceased owner's will, unlike a tenancy in common.

question: To create a valid joint tenancy under common law, the co-owners generally must share which four unities?
choice_a: Marriage, age, income, and residency
choice_b: Time, title, interest, and possession
choice_c: Location, lien priority, tax status, and zoning
choice_d: Deed, mortgage, survey, and title insurance
explanation: A common-law joint tenancy traditionally requires four unities: the interests must be acquired at the same time, under the same title/document, with equal interests, and with equal rights of possession; most states also require the joint tenancy to be expressly stated in the deed.

question: Which form of co-ownership is available only to married couples (or in some states, registered domestic partners) and provides survivorship rights along with protection from an individual spouse's separate creditors?
choice_a: Tenancy in common
choice_b: Ownership in severalty
choice_c: Tenancy by the entirety
choice_d: A cooperative ownership interest
explanation: Tenancy by the entirety is a special form of co-ownership recognized in some states, available only to married couples, that includes the right of survivorship and generally protects the property from claims by one spouse's individual creditors, since neither spouse can convey their interest without the other's consent.

question: In a condominium, how is ownership of the individual units and the shared amenities structured?
choice_a: Each owner holds shares in a corporation that owns the entire building, along with a proprietary lease to occupy a unit
choice_b: All owners collectively hold a single joint tenancy over the entire building with no individual unit ownership
choice_c: Ownership is limited to a right to use a unit for one specified week per year
choice_d: Each owner holds separate fee simple title to their individual unit's airspace, combined with an undivided tenancy-in-common interest in the common elements shared by all owners
explanation: Condominium ownership combines individual fee simple ownership of a specific unit (typically described as airspace) with an undivided tenancy-in-common ownership interest, alongside all other unit owners, in the building's common elements such as hallways, roofs, and grounds.

question: How does ownership in a housing cooperative differ from ownership in a condominium?
choice_a: In a cooperative, a corporation holds title to the entire building, and residents own shares of stock in the corporation along with a proprietary lease to occupy their unit, rather than owning real property directly
choice_b: In a cooperative, each resident holds fee simple title to their individual unit, identical to a condominium
choice_c: Cooperatives are always structured as joint tenancies among residents
choice_d: There is no legal or practical difference between the two forms of ownership
explanation: In a cooperative, the building itself is owned by a corporation; residents do not own real property directly but instead own shares of the corporation's stock and hold a proprietary lease granting the right to occupy a specific unit.

question: A buyer purchases the right to use a resort condominium for one specified week every year. What kind of ownership interest is this?
choice_a: A tenancy by the entirety
choice_b: A timeshare interest
choice_c: Ownership in severalty
choice_d: A life estate
explanation: A timeshare grants an owner the right to use a property, often a resort unit, for a specific, recurring period each year; timeshares can be structured either as fee-simple interval ownership or as a right-to-use arrangement, depending on how they are created.

question: When real property is held in trust, who holds legal title, and who benefits from the property?
choice_a: The beneficiary holds legal title, and the trustee has no rights to the property at all
choice_b: The person who created the trust automatically loses all rights and interests in the property
choice_c: A trustee holds legal title and manages the property for the benefit of a beneficiary, who holds equitable title
choice_d: Legal and equitable title are always held by the same single person in a trust
explanation: In a property trust arrangement, the trustor (or settlor) transfers legal title to a trustee, who manages the property according to the trust's terms for the benefit of a designated beneficiary, who holds equitable title and the beneficial interest in the property.

question: After a property owner dies, who typically has legal authority to manage and eventually convey the deceased owner's real property during probate?
choice_a: Any licensed real estate broker chosen by the heirs
choice_b: The county tax assessor
choice_c: The deceased owner's mortgage lender
choice_d: An executor named in the will, or a court-appointed administrator if there is no valid will
explanation: When someone dies leaving a valid will, the will typically names an executor to administer the estate; if there is no will (intestate), a court appoints an administrator to perform that role, including managing and eventually distributing or conveying the decedent's real property under court supervision.

question: When real property is titled in the name of a corporation, how is that ownership generally characterized?
choice_a: As ownership in severalty, since the corporation is treated as a single legal entity in its own right, separate from its individual shareholders
choice_b: As a joint tenancy among all of the corporation's shareholders
choice_c: As a tenancy in common among the corporation's board members
choice_d: As a life estate held collectively by the shareholders
explanation: A corporation is a distinct legal entity that can own property in its own name; because it is treated as a single owner, property titled to a corporation is considered ownership in severalty, even though many individual shareholders own the corporation itself.

question: How does a general partnership's ownership of real property typically expose the partners to liability?
choice_a: General partners have no personal liability whatsoever for partnership obligations
choice_b: Each general partner can be held personally liable for partnership debts and obligations related to the property, without the liability protection offered by a corporation or LLC
choice_c: Only the partnership's largest investor bears any liability
choice_d: Partnerships cannot legally own real property under any circumstances
explanation: In a general partnership, each general partner shares personal liability for the debts and obligations of the partnership, including those tied to jointly owned real property, unlike shareholders of a corporation or members of an LLC, who typically enjoy limited liability.

question: Why do investors commonly choose to hold real property through a limited liability company (LLC)?
choice_a: An LLC eliminates the need to ever record a deed
choice_b: An LLC automatically grants its members a life estate in any property it owns
choice_c: An LLC generally combines the limited personal liability protection of a corporation with more flexible, pass-through tax treatment similar to a partnership
choice_d: An LLC is legally identical to a joint tenancy
explanation: A limited liability company is a popular vehicle for holding investment real estate because it generally shields individual members from personal liability for the entity's debts, similar to a corporation, while typically allowing profits and losses to pass through to members for tax purposes, similar to a partnership.

question: A life estate grants an owner, called the life tenant, the right to possess and use property for a duration measured by which of the following?
choice_a: A fixed term of exactly 99 years
choice_b: As long as the life tenant continues to pay rent to a landlord
choice_c: Until the property is sold to a third party, regardless of anyone's lifespan
choice_d: The life tenant's own lifetime, or in some cases, the lifetime of another named person
explanation: A life estate is an ownership interest that lasts for the duration of a specified life; when it is measured by the life tenant's own life it is a standard life estate, and when measured by the life of a different named person it is called a life estate pur autre vie.

question: When a life estate ends because the measuring life has ended, what happens to the property if the original grant named a specific third party to receive it?
choice_a: The property passes to that named third party, called the remainderman, who holds a remainder interest
choice_b: The property is automatically sold at public auction
choice_c: The property escheats to the state regardless of the grant's terms
choice_d: The life tenant's heirs always inherit the property instead
explanation: If the grantor names a specific person to receive full ownership once the life estate ends, that person holds what is called a remainder interest and is known as the remainderman; upon the life tenant's death (or the death of the measuring life), title passes automatically to the remainderman.

question: If a life estate is created without naming a remainderman, what happens to the property when the life estate ends?
choice_a: The life tenant's estate keeps the property permanently
choice_b: The property reverts back to the original grantor or the grantor's heirs, a future interest called a reversion
choice_c: Ownership converts automatically to a joint tenancy
choice_d: The property is deemed abandoned and available for adverse possession claims only
explanation: When no remainderman is named, the grantor retains a future interest called a reversion, meaning full ownership automatically returns to the grantor (or the grantor's heirs) once the life estate terminates.

question: What legal obligation does a life tenant have regarding the property during the life estate?
choice_a: The life tenant has no obligations at all and may destroy the property freely
choice_b: The life tenant must transfer full fee simple title within one year
choice_c: The life tenant must avoid committing waste, meaning they cannot take actions that permanently damage the property or diminish its value for the remainderman or reversioner
choice_d: The life tenant is exempt from paying any property-related expenses
explanation: A life tenant has a duty not to commit waste, meaning they must maintain the property in reasonable condition and generally cannot take actions, such as destructive alterations, that would permanently reduce the property's value for the remainderman or the party holding the reversion.

question: A deed grants Owner A a life estate 'for the life of Owner B.' If Owner A dies before Owner B, what happens to the life estate?
choice_a: The life estate immediately and permanently ends upon Owner A's death
choice_b: The property immediately reverts to the grantor upon Owner A's death
choice_c: Owner B automatically becomes the fee simple owner upon Owner A's death
choice_d: The life estate continues, and it passes to Owner A's heirs or estate until Owner B dies, since the measuring life is Owner B's, not Owner A's
explanation: This is a life estate pur autre vie, meaning the duration is measured by the life of a person other than the life tenant (here, Owner B). If Owner A dies first, the estate does not end; it passes to Owner A's heirs or estate and continues until Owner B, the measuring life, dies.

question: Private, recorded restrictions placed on how land within a subdivision may be used (such as limiting properties to single-family residential use) are best described as which of the following?
choice_a: Deed restrictions or restrictive covenants, which are a form of encumbrance that generally runs with the land
choice_b: Easements in gross benefiting a public utility
choice_c: A form of adverse possession
choice_d: A government zoning ordinance
explanation: Deed restrictions, also called restrictive covenants, are private limitations placed on the use of land, typically established by a developer and recorded against all lots in a subdivision; because they are recorded and tied to the land, they run with the land and bind future owners, functioning as an encumbrance distinct from public zoning laws.
